set_title: Polyuria, thirst and a sodium problem
stem: A 41-year-old man has passed about 6 liters of urine a day for 3 months and wakes four times a night to urinate. Fasting glucose is 92 mg/dL, serum sodium is 147 mEq/L and urine osmolality is 90 mOsm/kg. One hour after desmopressin, urine osmolality is 100 mOsm/kg.
oneliner: 41M + 6 L urine/day + nocturia + glucose 92 + Na 147 + urine osm 90 → 100 after desmopressin → ?
ask: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Central DI would make urine osmolality **rise by more than 50% after desmopressin**; his went only from 90 to 100
whyNot.B: Primary polydipsia gives a **low-normal sodium**; his is 147, so he is losing water, not drinking too much
whyNot.D: SIADH gives a **low sodium with concentrated urine**; he has a high sodium with urine at 90 mOsm/kg
whyNot.E: Osmotic diuresis needs **high blood glucose**; his fasting glucose is 92

why: High sodium with very dilute urine means water is lost through the kidney. **Desmopressin barely changes the urine**, so ADH is not the missing piece: the collecting duct cannot respond to it.

High-normal or high
Dilute (often below 200 mOsm/kg)

Nephrogenic diabetes insipidus

**Stays dilute even after desmopressin** (ADH already high)
Lithium, hypercalcemia, V2 receptor mutation

Low-normal or low
Dilute
**Concentrates when water is withheld**; little further rise with desmopressin
Psychiatric illness, drinks large volumes

**Inappropriately concentrated (above 100 mOsm/kg) with urine sodium above 40 mEq/L**
Not needed: no polyuria

Not needed

idea.rule: Dilute urine + high sodium = DI; desmopressin works → central, desmopressin fails → nephrogenic.
also: Lithium is the classic cause of nephrogenic DI; thiazides or amiloride treat it

set_title: Hypersensitivity types I to IV
stem: A 24-year-old man has hemoptysis and rapidly progressive glomerulonephritis. Renal biopsy shows crescents and IgG in the glomeruli. Type II and type III hypersensitivity are both being considered.
oneliner: 24M + hemoptysis + rapidly progressive GN + crescents + glomerular IgG → type II or type III?
ask: Which single finding favours type II over type III?

options.E: Linear staining of IgG along the basement membrane

whyNot.A: **Crescents** form in both when the glomerulus is severely injured
whyNot.B: A **low C3** favours type III, where complexes consume complement; it is typically normal in anti-GBM disease
whyNot.C: **IgG in the glomerulus** is present in both; only the pattern differs
whyNot.D: **Hematuria with proteinuria** occurs in both

answer: Linear staining of IgG along the basement membrane
why: In type II, antibody binds a **fixed antigen** (here the alpha-3 chain of type IV collagen), producing a smooth linear ribbon. In type III, circulating complexes lodge unevenly and look **granular or lumpy**.

set_title: Edema or ascites with raised or normal neck veins: which pump or organ
stem: A 7-year-old boy has puffy eyes and leg swelling. Heart failure and nephrotic syndrome are both being considered.
oneliner: 7M + periorbital and leg edema → heart failure or nephrotic syndrome?
ask: Which single finding favours nephrotic syndrome over heart failure?

whyNot.A: **Pitting edema** occurs in both
whyNot.B: **Weight gain** from fluid occurs in both
whyNot.D: **Evening-worse edema** from gravity occurs in both
whyNot.E: **Low urine sodium** from RAAS activation occurs in both

why: Nephrotic edema comes from albumin lost in the urine, which lowers plasma oncotic pressure, not from a failing pump. **Proteinuria above 3.5 g/day** defines it; heart failure gives at most mild proteinuria, plus a raised JVP and crackles.

set_title: High hematocrit: polycythemia vera or a secondary cause
stem: A 60-year-old man has had 4 months of headaches and a ruddy face. Hematocrit is 60% and oxygen saturation on room air is 97%. Serum erythropoietin is high.
oneliner: 60M + headaches and ruddy face + hematocrit 60% + oxygen saturation 97% + high erythropoietin → ?
ask: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.B: Essential thrombocythemia is a platelet disorder; his abnormality is a **hematocrit of 60% with high erythropoietin**
whyNot.C: Polycythemia vera suppresses erythropoietin; his is **high**
whyNot.D: Hypoxia needs a low saturation; his is **97%**
whyNot.E: Chronic myeloid leukemia raises the leukocyte count; his abnormality is a **hematocrit of 60% with high erythropoietin**

why: Same man, one change: **erythropoietin is high with a normal oxygen saturation**. Hypoxia is excluded, so the hormone is coming from a tumor. Renal cell carcinoma is the commonest source, and hematuria, a flank mass and weight loss would complete the picture.

Normal
**Low** (the marrow acts without erythropoietin)

**Low** (COPD, high altitude, sleep apnea, right-to-left shunt)
High (an appropriate response to hypoxia)
JAK2 negative; no splenomegaly; leukocytes and platelets normal
Heavy smoking, COPD or altitude; oxygen lowers the hematocrit
Renal cell carcinoma (erythropoietin-secreting)
Normal
**High, made inappropriately by the tumor**
JAK2 negative; no splenomegaly
Hematuria, flank pain, palpable mass, weight loss

idea.rule: High hematocrit, normal saturation, high erythropoietin = an erythropoietin-secreting tumor, such as renal cell carcinoma.
also: Hepatocellular carcinoma and cerebellar hemangioblastoma also make erythropoietin
Renal cell carcinoma can also cause hypercalcemia and a varicocele
Clear cells with lipid and glycogen; VHL loss

set_title: Creatinine rising over days: prerenal, tubular, interstitial, drug hemodynamics or a blocked outlet
stem: A 62-year-old man has had vomiting and watery diarrhea for 4 days. His blood pressure is 94/56 mm Hg, pulse is 114/min, and his mucous membranes are dry. Serum creatinine is 2.1 mg/dL (baseline 0.9 mg/dL). The urine has a specific gravity of 1.031 and no casts, and the fractional excretion of sodium is 0.4%.
oneliner: 62M + 4 days of vomiting and diarrhea + BP 94/56 + dry mucosa + creatinine 0.9→2.1 + specific gravity 1.031 + no casts + FENa 0.4% → ?
ask: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: AIN follows a **new drug with fever and rash** and shows white cell casts; he has **no drug, rash or casts**
whyNot.B: ATN gives **muddy brown casts and a FENa above 2%**; his urine has **no casts and a FENa of 0.4%**
whyNot.D: Obstruction would not explain the **dry mucous membranes and low blood pressure** from 4 days of fluid loss
whyNot.E: This needs **NSAID or ACE inhibitor exposure**, and **none is described**; his cause is **vomiting and diarrhea**

why: Four days of fluid loss lower renal perfusion, so intact tubules hold on to sodium and water. A **FENa below 1% with concentrated, cast-free urine** means prerenal azotemia, and saline reverses it. The BUN:creatinine ratio is above 20 for the same reason: urea is reabsorbed with water.

stem: A 67-year-old woman has 2 hours of mean arterial pressure below 60 mm Hg during emergency repair of a ruptured abdominal aortic aneurysm, restored with transfusions. Over the next 3 days urine output through an indwelling bladder catheter is 15 mL/h. Creatinine rises from 1.0 to 4.2 mg/dL and does not fall after 2 L of saline. Urine osmolality is 300 mOsm/kg and urine sodium is 62 mEq/L.
oneliner: 67F + 2 h of hypotension in aneurysm repair + catheter output 15 mL/h + creatinine 1.0→4.2 + no response to 2 L saline + urine osm 300 + urine Na 62 → ?
ask: Which of the following is the most likely diagnosis?

whyNot.A: Prerenal azotemia gives **urine sodium below 20 and osmolality above 500** and improves with saline; hers shows **sodium 62, osmolality 300 and no response to 2 L**
whyNot.B: The **indwelling bladder catheter** excludes an outlet obstruction, and ischemia from **2 hours of hypotension** is the cause
whyNot.C: This needs an NSAID or ACE inhibitor, **none described**; she had **an ischemic insult during surgery**

stem: A 44-year-old woman, gravida 3, para 3, has had 8 months of urine leakage. She leaks small amounts when she coughs, laughs or lifts heavy boxes, and never at night. Pelvic examination shows no prolapse and the bladder is not distended. Urinalysis is normal.

stem: A newborn boy has an enlarged, cystic left kidney on ultrasonography; the right kidney has not yet been imaged.
oneliner: Newborn M + enlarged cystic left kidney + right kidney not yet imaged → ?
ask: Which single finding would favor autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease over multicystic dysplastic kidney?

whyNot.A: Both conditions can occur with **unaffected parents** (carriers in one, sporadic in the other)
whyNot.B: An enlarged kidney in a newborn can be felt as a **flank mass** in either
whyNot.D: Cysts in both are lined by epithelium, so this does not separate them in a **cystic kidney**
whyNot.E: A normal right kidney would point toward the **unilateral** disease, away from autosomal recessive polycystic disease

why: Fibrocystin (PKHD1) defects affect both the kidney and the bile ducts, so autosomal recessive polycystic disease carries congenital hepatic fibrosis and later portal hypertension. A multicystic dysplastic kidney is a sporadic, usually unilateral lesion with no liver involvement. **Liver fibrosis beside cystic kidneys means autosomal recessive polycystic kidney disease.**
